overactive_bladder.desc: The muscle of the bladder wall contracts before the bladder is full.
overactive_bladder.symptoms: Sudden strong urges, frequent urination day and night, sometimes leaking.
overactive_bladder.causes: Often no clear cause; it can come with nervous system diseases and with age.
overactive_bladder.treatment: Bladder training, pelvic floor exercises, medicines that relax the bladder wall.

bladder_stones.name: Bladder stones
bladder_stones.desc: Stones form in the bladder itself when urine stays in it too long.
bladder_stones.symptoms: Lower abdominal pain, a stop-start stream, blood in the urine, frequent urges.
bladder_stones.causes: Incomplete emptying of the bladder, in men most often due to an enlarged prostate; stones coming down from the kidneys.
bladder_stones.treatment: Breaking up and removing them with a scope, and treating the cause of urine retention.

incontinence.name: Urinary incontinence
incontinence.symptoms: Leaking when coughing, laughing or exercising (stress incontinence), or with a sudden strong urge (urge incontinence).
incontinence.causes: Weak pelvic floor muscles after childbirth and with age, overactive bladder, prostate and nervous system diseases.
incontinence.treatment: Pelvic floor exercises, medicines, surgery; it can be treated, and there is no need to feel embarrassed seeing a doctor.

esophagitis.name: Esophagitis
esophagitis.desc: Inflammation of the lining of the esophagus.
esophagitis.symptoms: Heartburn, pain behind the breastbone, pain and difficulty when swallowing.
esophagitis.causes: Most often GERD; also infections, allergy (eosinophilic esophagitis), tablets that get stuck in the esophagus.
esophagitis.treatment: Treating the cause: lowering stomach acid, antifungal drugs, a special diet for allergy.

barrett.name: Barrett's esophagus
barrett.desc: Under the effect of acid, the lining of the lower esophagus changes and comes to look like the lining of the intestine.
barrett.symptoms: No signs of its own, only long-lasting heartburn from GERD.
barrett.causes: Years of stomach contents flowing back; more common in men over 50 with excess weight.
barrett.treatment: Controlling GERD and regular gastroscopy: the changes raise the risk of esophageal cancer and can be removed through a scope.

hiatal_hernia.name: Hiatal hernia
hiatal_hernia.desc: Part of the stomach slides through the opening in the diaphragm from the abdomen into the chest.
hiatal_hernia.symptoms: Often none; otherwise heartburn, burping, pain behind the breastbone, especially lying down.
hiatal_hernia.causes: Tissues weakening with age, raised pressure in the abdomen: excess weight, pregnancy, straining.
hiatal_hernia.treatment: Treating reflux; large hernias are repaired with surgery.

tracheitis.name: Tracheitis
tracheitis.desc: Inflammation of the lining of the trachea, usually together with laryngitis or bronchitis.
tracheitis.symptoms: A dry, tiring cough, a raw feeling behind the breastbone, fever.
tracheitis.causes: Most often cold and flu viruses, less often bacteria; irritation from smoke and cold air.
tracheitis.treatment: It usually clears up on its own: warm drinks, humid air; antibiotics for a bacterial infection.

tracheal_stenosis.name: Tracheal stenosis
tracheal_stenosis.desc: The trachea narrows because of a scar or a tumour, and air passes through it with difficulty.
tracheal_stenosis.symptoms: Breathlessness and noisy, whistling breathing (stridor) that slowly get worse.
tracheal_stenosis.causes: Most often scarring after a long time on a ventilator or after a tracheostomy, less often tumours.
tracheal_stenosis.treatment: Widening the narrow part through a bronchoscope, a stent, or removing that section of the trachea.

sources.name: Merck Manual Consumer Version: Laryngotracheal Stenosis

foreign_body.name: Inhaled foreign body
foreign_body.desc: An object or piece of food gets into the larynx, trachea or bronchi.
foreign_body.symptoms: Sudden coughing, choking, being unable to speak; if the object moves into a bronchus, a long-lasting cough and pneumonia.
foreign_body.causes: More common in small children (nuts, small toys) and older people; talking and laughing while eating.
foreign_body.treatment: For choking, the Heimlich manoeuvre (thrusts into the upper abdomen). A stuck object is removed with a bronchoscope.

sources.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Foreign object - inhaled

tracheomalacia.name: Tracheomalacia
tracheomalacia.desc: The cartilage of the trachea is too soft, so the tube collapses when breathing out or coughing.
tracheomalacia.symptoms: Noisy breathing, a barking cough, frequent chest infections; in babies from the first weeks of life.
tracheomalacia.causes: Immature cartilage from birth; in adults, after a long intubation or pressure from a tumour or goitre.
tracheomalacia.treatment: In children it usually goes away by age 2–3; severe cases need stents or surgery.

addison.name: Adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)
addison.desc: The adrenal cortex makes too little cortisol and aldosterone.
addison.symptoms: Weakness, weight loss, low blood pressure, craving salt, darkening of the skin.
addison.causes: Most often the immune system destroys the adrenal cortex; less often tuberculosis.
addison.treatment: Lifelong hormone tablets to replace the missing ones; the dose is raised during stress and illness.

cushing.name: Cushing's syndrome
cushing.desc: There is too much cortisol in the body.
cushing.symptoms: A round face, belly fat with thin arms and legs, purple stretch marks, high blood pressure, weak muscles, diabetes.
cushing.causes: Most often long-term use of steroid medicines; less often a tumour of the pituitary or an adrenal gland.
cushing.treatment: Gradually stopping the steroids if possible, or removing the tumour.

pheochromocytoma.name: Pheochromocytoma
pheochromocytoma.desc: A tumour of the adrenal medulla that releases adrenaline and noradrenaline into the blood.
pheochromocytoma.symptoms: Episodes of a sharp rise in blood pressure, pounding heartbeat, headache, sweating, pale skin.
pheochromocytoma.causes: Usually no clear cause; some cases are inherited.
pheochromocytoma.treatment: Removing the tumour after preparation with medicines that lower blood pressure.

conn.name: Primary aldosteronism (Conn's syndrome)
conn.desc: The adrenal glands make too much aldosterone.
conn.symptoms: Persistent high blood pressure that is hard to treat; low potassium causing weakness and cramps.
conn.causes: A small benign tumour of one adrenal gland or overgrowth of both adrenal glands.
conn.treatment: Removing the adrenal gland with the tumour, or medicines that block aldosterone.

sources.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Primary and secondary hyperaldosteronism

appendix_tumors.name: Appendiceal tumors
appendix_tumors.desc: Rare tumours of the appendix; the most common is a neuroendocrine tumour, usually small and harmless.
appendix_tumors.symptoms: Usually none; they are often found by chance after the appendix is removed.
appendix_tumors.treatment: Removing the appendix, and for large tumours part of the large intestine.

sources.name: National Cancer Institute: Gastrointestinal Neuroendocrine Tumors Treatment

mucocele.name: Appendiceal mucocele
mucocele.desc: The appendix becomes swollen with mucus trapped inside it.
mucocele.symptoms: Usually none; sometimes pain in the lower right abdomen, like appendicitis.
mucocele.causes: A blocked opening or a mucus-producing tumour.
mucocele.treatment: Careful removal: if the mucocele bursts, the mucus can spread through the abdominal cavity.

sources.name: PubMed Central: Mucocele of the appendix: case report of a rare disease with changing diagnostic-therapeutic behavior

hemorrhoids.name: Hemorrhoids
hemorrhoids.desc: Clusters of blood vessels in the lower rectum swell, become inflamed and can prolapse.
hemorrhoids.symptoms: Bright red blood on the paper after a bowel movement, itching, lumps that come out, pain if a lump clots.
hemorrhoids.causes: Constipation and straining, long sitting, pregnancy, too little fibre.
hemorrhoids.treatment: Fibre and water, suppositories and creams; lumps can be banded with rubber rings or removed.

anal_fissure.name: Anal fissure
anal_fissure.desc: A small tear in the lining of the anus.
anal_fissure.symptoms: Sharp pain during and after a bowel movement, a little bright red blood.
anal_fissure.causes: Hard stools and constipation, less often diarrhoea.
anal_fissure.treatment: Soft stools thanks to fibre, warm baths, creams that relax the sphincter; surgery is rarely needed.

proctitis.name: Proctitis
proctitis.desc: Inflammation of the lining of the rectum.
proctitis.symptoms: Frequent false urges, mucus and blood in the stool, pain in the anus.
proctitis.causes: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, infections, radiotherapy to the pelvis.
proctitis.treatment: Treating the cause: anti-inflammatory suppositories and enemas, antibiotics for infections.

fibroids.name: Uterine fibroids
fibroids.desc: Benign tumours of the uterine muscle; very common, many women have them by age 50.
fibroids.symptoms: Often none; otherwise heavy, long periods, pelvic heaviness, frequent urges from pressure on the bladder.
fibroids.causes: They grow under the influence of estrogen; family history matters.
fibroids.treatment: Watching, hormone medicines, removing the fibroids or blocking the arteries that feed them. After menopause they usually shrink.

endometriosis.name: Endometriosis
endometriosis.desc: Tissue similar to the endometrium grows outside the uterus: on the ovaries, the lining of the abdomen, the bowel.
endometriosis.symptoms: Very painful periods, pelvic pain, difficulty getting pregnant.
endometriosis.causes: The exact cause is unknown; one theory is menstrual blood flowing back through the fallopian tubes.
endometriosis.treatment: Painkillers, hormone medicines, removing the patches during laparoscopy.

cervical_cancer.name: Cervical cancer
cervical_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the cervix; it is almost always caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV).
cervical_cancer.symptoms: No signs early on; later, bleeding after sex or between periods.
cervical_cancer.causes: Long-term infection with high-risk HPV types, smoking.
cervical_cancer.treatment: The HPV vaccine and regular smear tests prevent most cases. Treatment: surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

endometritis.name: Endometritis
endometritis.desc: Inflammation of the inner lining of the uterus, the endometrium.
endometritis.symptoms: Lower abdominal pain, fever, unusual discharge.
endometritis.causes: Infection after childbirth, abortion or procedures inside the uterus, sexually transmitted infections.

pcos.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
pcos.desc: A hormonal disorder: the ovaries have many immature follicles and ovulation is rare.
pcos.symptoms: Irregular or infrequent periods, acne, excess hair growth, weight gain, difficulty getting pregnant.
pcos.causes: Excess male hormones and insulin resistance; family history.
pcos.treatment: Weight loss, hormone medicines, drugs for insulin resistance, ovulation induction.

sources.name: WHO fact sheet: Polycystic ovary syndrome

ovarian_cyst.name: Ovarian cyst
ovarian_cyst.desc: A fluid-filled sac in an ovary; most often a functional cyst from a follicle or the corpus luteum.
ovarian_cyst.symptoms: Usually none; a large cyst causes heaviness and pelvic pain.
ovarian_cyst.causes: A follicle did not burst at ovulation or the corpus luteum filled with fluid; less often endometriosis or tumours.
ovarian_cyst.treatment: Functional cysts go away on their own within 1–3 cycles; persistent and large ones are removed.

ovarian_cancer.name: Ovarian cancer
ovarian_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the ovary; it is often found late.
ovarian_cancer.symptoms: Vague signs: bloating and a growing belly, feeling full quickly, pelvic pain.
ovarian_cancer.causes: Age, family history (BRCA gene mutations), endometriosis.
ovarian_cancer.treatment: Surgery and chemotherapy; carriers of BRCA mutations sometimes have the ovaries and tubes removed as a precaution.

ovarian_apoplexy.name: Ovarian apoplexy
ovarian_apoplexy.desc: A sudden rupture of an ovary with bleeding, usually at ovulation or from the corpus luteum.
ovarian_apoplexy.symptoms: Sharp pain on one side of the lower abdomen, weakness, dizziness with heavy bleeding.
ovarian_apoplexy.causes: A burst vessel in a follicle or the corpus luteum, sometimes after exercise or sex.
ovarian_apoplexy.treatment: Observation for light bleeding; surgery that saves the ovary for heavy bleeding.

sources.name: PubMed Central: Hemorrhagic corpus luteum: Clinical management update

prostatitis.name: Prostatitis
prostatitis.desc: Inflammation of the prostate, either an acute bacterial infection or a long-lasting condition.
prostatitis.symptoms: Pain between the legs and in the lower abdomen, frequent painful urination, fever in acute cases.
prostatitis.causes: Bacteria; in the chronic form the cause is often unclear.
prostatitis.treatment: Antibiotics for bacterial prostatitis; painkillers, relaxing medicines and physiotherapy for the chronic form.

bph.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
bph.desc: With age the prostate grows and squeezes the urethra.
bph.symptoms: A weak, stop-start stream, frequent urges, especially at night, a feeling that the bladder is not empty.
bph.causes: Age and male hormones: most men over 60 have it.
bph.treatment: Medicines that relax the bladder neck or shrink the gland; surgery if the squeezing is severe.

prostate_cancer.name: Prostate cancer
prostate_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the prostate; it often grows very slowly.
prostate_cancer.symptoms: No signs in the early stages; later, difficulty urinating and bone pain.
prostate_cancer.treatment: A PSA blood test and MRI help find it early. Slow tumours are watched, others are treated with surgery, radiotherapy or hormones.

aortic_aneurysm.name: Aortic aneurysm
aortic_aneurysm.desc: The aortic wall weakens and bulges out like a balloon. A large aneurysm can burst, causing life-threatening bleeding.
aortic_aneurysm.symptoms: Often none; it is found on an ultrasound. Sometimes a pulsing lump in the abdomen or pain in the belly or back.
aortic_aneurysm.causes: Atherosclerosis, high blood pressure, smoking, older age, inherited connective-tissue disorders.
aortic_aneurysm.treatment: A small one is watched with ultrasound and blood pressure is treated; a large one is replaced with a graft, by surgery or a stent-graft put in through an artery.

aortic_dissection.name: Aortic dissection
aortic_dissection.desc: Blood forces its way through a tear in the inner layer of the aorta and splits its wall apart. A medical emergency.
aortic_dissection.symptoms: Sudden tearing pain in the chest or back that may move; weakness, fainting, different blood pressure in the two arms.
aortic_dissection.causes: High blood pressure, atherosclerosis, inherited connective-tissue disorders (Marfan syndrome), injury.
aortic_dissection.treatment: Emergency care: blood pressure and heart rate are lowered; if the ascending part is affected, urgent surgery.

atherosclerosis.name: Atherosclerosis
atherosclerosis.desc: Plaques of fat and cholesterol build up in artery walls: the channel narrows and blood flow weakens.
atherosclerosis.symptoms: Unnoticed for a long time. Later it depends on where the narrowing is: chest pain on exertion, leg pain when walking, signs of stroke.
atherosclerosis.causes: Smoking, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, diabetes, excess weight, inactivity, age.
atherosclerosis.treatment: Quitting smoking, exercise, less animal fat in the diet; medicines for cholesterol and blood pressure; a stent or bypass for severe narrowing.

coarctation.name: Coarctation of the aorta
coarctation.desc: A narrowing of the aorta present from birth, usually just after the arch: pressure is high above it and low below it.
coarctation.symptoms: High blood pressure in the arms and a weak pulse in the legs, headaches, cold feet; in babies, fast breathing and poor weight gain.
coarctation.causes: The vessel develops abnormally before birth; it often comes with other heart defects.
coarctation.treatment: The narrowing is widened with a balloon and stent or removed by surgery; blood pressure is then checked for life.

sources.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Coarctation of the aorta

svc_syndrome.name: Superior vena cava syndrome
svc_syndrome.desc: The superior vena cava is squeezed or blocked, so blood from the head, neck and arms cannot drain properly to the heart.
svc_syndrome.symptoms: Swelling of the face, neck and arms, bulging veins on the neck and chest, shortness of breath, cough, headache, worse when lying down.
svc_syndrome.causes: Most often a tumor in the chest (lung cancer, lymphoma); less often a clot around a catheter or pacemaker lead.
svc_syndrome.treatment: The cause is treated (chemotherapy or radiotherapy for a tumor), clots are dissolved with medicines; the vein can be opened with a stent.

sources.name: Cleveland Clinic: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome (SVCS)

ivc_thrombosis.name: Inferior vena cava thrombosis
ivc_thrombosis.desc: A blood clot partly or fully blocks the inferior vena cava; it often spreads up from clots in the leg or pelvic veins.
ivc_thrombosis.symptoms: Swelling and heaviness in both legs, enlarged veins on the belly, lower back pain; a piece of clot can break off and reach the lungs.
ivc_thrombosis.causes: Long immobility, surgery, tumors, pregnancy, blood that clots too easily, a filter placed in the vein.
ivc_thrombosis.treatment: Medicines that stop blood from clotting (anticoagulants); sometimes the clot is dissolved or removed through a catheter.

sources.name: StatPearls, NCBI Bookshelf: Inferior vena cava syndrome

spinal_injury.name: Spinal cord injury
spinal_injury.desc: Damage to the spinal cord when the spine is injured: signals below the injury stop getting through.
spinal_injury.symptoms: Weakness or paralysis and loss of feeling below the level of injury, problems with breathing (neck injuries), bowels and bladder.
spinal_injury.causes: Road accidents, falls from height, diving into shallow water, sports injuries, wounds.
spinal_injury.treatment: Keeping the spine still right after the injury, urgent surgery, then long rehabilitation. A person who may have a spinal injury should not be moved unless necessary.

sources.name: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: Spinal cord trauma

herniated_disc.name: Herniated disc
herniated_disc.desc: The jelly-like core of a disc between vertebrae bulges out through a crack and presses on a nerve root.
herniated_disc.symptoms: Pain in the lower back or neck that spreads into a leg or arm, numbness, tingling, muscle weakness.
herniated_disc.causes: Wear of the discs with age, lifting heavy things while bending, excess weight, sitting a lot, injury.
herniated_disc.treatment: Usually gets better without surgery: painkillers, exercises, physiotherapy; surgery if a nerve is badly compressed.

multiple_sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple_sclerosis.desc: The immune system damages the coating of nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord, so signals pass less well.
multiple_sclerosis.symptoms: Episodes of blurred vision, numbness, weakness in the arms and legs, unsteadiness, severe tiredness; it may improve between episodes.
multiple_sclerosis.causes: An autoimmune disease; the risk rises with family history, low vitamin D, smoking and past Epstein–Barr virus infection.
multiple_sclerosis.treatment: There is no cure yet, but medicines reduce flare-ups and slow the disease; steroids for flare-ups, rehabilitation.

carpal_tunnel.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
carpal_tunnel.desc: The median nerve is squeezed in a narrow tunnel in the wrist.
carpal_tunnel.symptoms: Numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, especially at night; weakness of the hand.
carpal_tunnel.causes: Repetitive hand movements, pregnancy, diabetes, an underactive thyroid, rheumatoid arthritis, wrist injuries.
carpal_tunnel.treatment: A wrist splint at night, breaks from work, sometimes steroid injections; if that fails, surgery to free the nerve.

myasthenia.name: Myasthenia gravis
myasthenia.desc: The immune system makes antibodies that block nerves from passing commands to muscles. It is often linked to the thymus.
myasthenia.symptoms: Muscle weakness that gets worse in the evening and after effort: drooping eyelids, double vision, trouble chewing and swallowing.
myasthenia.causes: An autoimmune disease; many patients have an enlarged thymus or a thymus tumor (thymoma).
myasthenia.treatment: Medicines that boost signal transmission and drugs that calm the immune system; the thymus is often removed by surgery.

thymoma.name: Thymoma
thymoma.desc: A tumor of thymus cells that usually grows slowly.
thymoma.symptoms: Often none; it is found on a chest scan. Sometimes cough, pain behind the breastbone, shortness of breath or signs of myasthenia gravis.
thymoma.causes: The cause is unknown; it is most common at 40–60 years of age.
thymoma.treatment: Removal of the thymus together with the tumor, plus radiotherapy or chemotherapy if needed.

sources.name: National Cancer Institute: Thymoma and Thymic Carcinoma

pituitary_adenoma.name: Pituitary adenoma
pituitary_adenoma.desc: A benign tumor of the pituitary. It may release extra hormones or press on nearby nerves.
pituitary_adenoma.symptoms: Depends on the hormone: menstrual changes and nipple discharge, signs of acromegaly or Cushing's; a large tumor causes headaches and loss of side vision.
pituitary_adenoma.treatment: Some tumors shrink with medicines; others are removed by surgery through the nose, sometimes followed by radiotherapy.

acromegaly.name: Acromegaly
acromegaly.desc: An adult has too much growth hormone: the hands, feet, nose, jaw and internal organs get bigger.
acromegaly.symptoms: Rings and shoes get tight, facial features coarsen, gaps appear between the teeth, sweating, joint pain; in childhood the excess causes gigantism.
acromegaly.causes: Almost always a pituitary adenoma that releases growth hormone.
acromegaly.treatment: Surgery to remove the adenoma, medicines that block growth hormone, sometimes radiotherapy.

hypopituitarism.name: Hypopituitarism
hypopituitarism.desc: The pituitary releases too little of one or more hormones, so the glands it controls work less.
hypopituitarism.symptoms: Weakness, tiredness, feeling cold, low sex drive, menstrual changes; poor growth in children.
hypopituitarism.causes: Pituitary tumors and surgery, head injury, radiotherapy, bleeding into the pituitary.
hypopituitarism.treatment: Lifelong replacement of the missing hormones: thyroid, adrenal and sex hormones, growth hormone.

diabetes_insipidus.name: Diabetes insipidus
diabetes_insipidus.desc: There is not enough of the hormone vasopressin (or the kidneys do not respond to it), so the kidneys cannot hold on to water.
diabetes_insipidus.symptoms: A lot of pale urine, up to 10–20 liters a day, strong thirst, waking at night to urinate.
diabetes_insipidus.causes: Tumors and injuries around the pituitary and hypothalamus, surgery; less often inherited causes or kidney disease.
diabetes_insipidus.treatment: A vasopressin substitute (desmopressin) as tablets or nasal spray, drinking to thirst.

diaphragmatic_hernia.name: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
diaphragmatic_hernia.desc: A baby is born with a hole in the diaphragm, and abdominal organs move into the chest and keep the lungs from growing.
diaphragmatic_hernia.symptoms: Severe breathing trouble right after birth, bluish skin, a sunken belly.
diaphragmatic_hernia.causes: The diaphragm does not close completely while the baby develops; the exact cause is usually unknown.
diaphragmatic_hernia.treatment: Intensive breathing support after birth, then surgery to close the hole. It is often found on an ultrasound during pregnancy.

diaphragm_paralysis.name: Diaphragm paralysis
diaphragm_paralysis.desc: The diaphragm, or half of it, stops contracting because the phrenic nerve is damaged.
diaphragm_paralysis.symptoms: Shortness of breath on exertion and when lying flat, poor sleep; paralysis of one side sometimes causes no symptoms.
diaphragm_paralysis.causes: Heart and neck surgery, injuries, chest tumors, viral infections, nerve and muscle diseases.
diaphragm_paralysis.treatment: It often recovers on its own over months; breathing machines at night help, sometimes surgery or a nerve stimulator.

hiccups.name: Persistent hiccups
hiccups.desc: Hiccups are sudden involuntary contractions of the diaphragm, each followed by the vocal cords snapping shut. They usually stop within minutes; persistent hiccups last more than two days.
hiccups.symptoms: Repeated 'hic' sounds that get in the way of eating, talking and sleeping.
hiccups.causes: Ordinary hiccups: overeating, fizzy drinks, alcohol, excitement; persistent ones may come with reflux, nervous-system or kidney disease, or some medicines.
hiccups.treatment: Ordinary hiccups stop on their own or after holding your breath or sipping cold water; persistent ones are investigated and the cause treated, sometimes with medicines.

lymphadenitis.name: Lymphadenitis
lymphadenitis.desc: Inflammation of a lymph node, usually caused by an infection nearby.
lymphadenitis.symptoms: The node is swollen and tender, the skin over it may turn red; fever, weakness.
lymphadenitis.causes: Sore throat, bad teeth, cuts and boils on the skin, childhood infections, less often tuberculosis or cat-scratch disease.
lymphadenitis.treatment: The source of infection is treated, with antibiotics for bacterial inflammation; a node full of pus is drained by a surgeon.

lymphoma.name: Lymphoma
lymphoma.desc: A cancer of immune cells called lymphocytes. It grows in the lymph nodes, spleen and other organs.
lymphoma.symptoms: Painless swollen nodes in the neck, armpits or groin, night sweats, unexplained fever, weight loss, itchy skin.
lymphoma.causes: Usually unknown; the risk is higher with a weakened immune system and some viral infections.
lymphoma.treatment: Chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radiotherapy; many lymphomas can be cured.

lymphedema.name: Lymphedema
lymphedema.desc: Lymph does not drain well and builds up in the tissues, usually in an arm or leg.
lymphedema.symptoms: Lasting swelling, heaviness and tight skin; over time the skin hardens.
lymphedema.causes: Removal or radiotherapy of lymph nodes during cancer treatment, infections, injuries, lymphatic vessels that did not develop properly.
lymphedema.treatment: Hard to cure completely: lymphatic drainage massage, compression garments, exercises and skin care help.

skull.name: Skull
skull.desc: The bony box of the head: it protects the brain and sense organs and shapes the face.
skull.location: The head; the lower jaw is hinged to it, and the spine joins it from below

details.type: A set of flat and irregular bones: 8 bones of the cranium and 14 of the face.
details.parts: Cranium: frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid bones. Face: maxillae, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal and palatine bones, inferior nasal conchae, vomer and mandible.
details.joints: The vault bones are joined by sutures (coronal, sagittal, lambdoid); the mandible by the temporomandibular joints; the occipital bone by the atlanto-occipital joint with the first cervical vertebra.
details.muscles: Muscles of chewing (temporalis, masseter, pterygoids), muscles of facial expression, and the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius of the neck.

facts.bones: Made of 22 bones, not counting the tiny ear bones
facts.sutures: The bones of the vault are joined by fixed seams called sutures; a baby has soft spots called fontanelles between them

mandible.name: Lower jaw (mandible)
mandible.desc: The only movable bone of the skull: it holds the lower teeth and moves when you chew and talk.
mandible.location: The lower face; joined to the temporal bones by joints just in front of the ears

details.type: An unpaired bone of the facial skeleton.
details.parts: A body with an alveolar part for 16 teeth and two rami; each ramus has a coronoid process (for the temporalis) and a condylar process with a head for the joint. The mental nerves exit through the mental foramina.
details.joints: The temporomandibular joints: both heads move together — the jaw opens, protrudes and moves sideways.
details.muscles: The masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid raise the jaw; the lateral pterygoid protrudes it; the suprahyoid muscles lower it.

facts.strongest: The largest and strongest bone of the face
facts.bite: The chewing muscles can press its teeth together with a force of tens of kilograms

clavicle.name: Collarbone (clavicle)
clavicle.desc: An S-shaped strut between the breastbone and the shoulder blade that holds the shoulder away from the chest.
clavicle.location: Above the first rib at the base of the neck; easy to feel under the skin

details.type: A long S-shaped bone without a marrow cavity — the only bony link between the arm and the trunk.
details.parts: Sternal end, shaft and acromial end; the medial two thirds curve forward, the lateral third curves back.
details.joints: The sternoclavicular joint with the manubrium and the acromioclavicular joint with the acromion of the scapula.
details.muscles: Sternocleidomastoid, trapezius, deltoid, pectoralis major and subclavius.

facts.fracture: One of the most often broken bones, usually in a fall onto the shoulder or an outstretched hand
facts.first: It starts turning into bone earlier than any other bone, long before birth

scapula.name: Shoulder blade (scapula)
scapula.desc: A flat triangular bone on the back of the rib cage that links the arm to the trunk.
scapula.location: The back of the rib cage, from the 2nd to the 7th rib; from the front it shows at the shoulder, behind the ribs

details.type: Flat triangular bone.
details.parts: Three borders and three angles; at the back the spine of the scapula ends in the acromion, at the front is the coracoid process, and at the outer angle the glenoid cavity for the head of the humerus.
details.joints: The shoulder joint with the humerus and the acromioclavicular joint with the clavicle; there is no joint with the ribs — the scapula glides over the chest on muscles.
details.muscles: Trapezius, deltoid, the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), serratus anterior, the rhomboids, both heads of the biceps and the long head of the triceps.

facts.rib: Only muscles tie it to the rib cage, which is why the shoulder moves so freely
facts.wing: When serratus anterior is weak, the shoulder blade lifts off the back like a wing

sternum.name: Breastbone (sternum)
sternum.desc: A flat bone in the middle of the chest: the ribs attach to it by cartilage, and the collarbones at the top.
sternum.location: In the middle of the front of the chest, in front of the heart

details.type: A flat spongy bone with red marrow — bone marrow samples can be taken from it.
details.parts: Manubrium, body and xiphoid process. The angle between manubrium and body lies at the level of the 2nd ribs — ribs are counted from it.
details.joints: The sternoclavicular joints with the clavicles and joints with the cartilages of ribs 1–7.
details.muscles: Pectoralis major, sternocleidomastoid, rectus abdominis (to the xiphoid process) and the diaphragm.

facts.parts: Made of three parts: the handle, the body and the sword-shaped tip
facts.cpr: In CPR, rescuers press rhythmically on the lower half of the breastbone

ribs.name: Ribs
ribs.desc: Twelve pairs of curved bones forming the rib cage: they protect the heart and lungs and lift when you breathe in.
ribs.location: The chest: at the back the ribs join the spine; at the front most of them join the breastbone by cartilage

details.type: Long flat bones containing red marrow.
details.parts: Head, neck, tubercle and shaft with a groove along the lower edge for the intercostal vessels and nerve — which is why the chest wall is punctured along the upper edge of a rib.
details.joints: At the back, joints of the rib heads with the vertebral bodies and costotransverse joints. In front, the cartilages of ribs 1–7 join the sternum, ribs 8–10 join the cartilage above (the costal margin), ribs 11–12 are free.
details.muscles: Intercostal muscles, diaphragm, scalene muscles of the neck (to ribs 1–2), pectoralis major and minor, serratus anterior and abdominal muscles.

facts.pairs: 7 pairs of true ribs reach the breastbone, 3 pairs are false and 2 pairs are floating
facts.breath: The muscles between the ribs lift them and help the diaphragm when you breathe in

spine.name: Spine (vertebral column)
spine.desc: The body's support, made of vertebrae: it holds up the head and trunk and protects the spinal cord in its canal.
spine.location: Along the back, from the base of the skull to the sacrum and tailbone

details.type: The vertebrae are irregular bones of spongy bone.
details.parts: A vertebra has a body, an arch and seven processes — spinous, two transverse and four articular. The vertebral foramina line up into the canal for the spinal cord.
details.joints: Intervertebral discs (annulus fibrosus and nucleus pulposus), facet joints and ligaments; the first two cervical vertebrae — atlas and axis — let the head nod and turn.
details.muscles: Erector spinae, transversospinal muscles, trapezius, latissimus dorsi and psoas major.

facts.vertebrae: 7 neck, 12 chest and 5 lower-back vertebrae, with the sacrum and tailbone below
facts.curves: Four curves turn it into a spring that cushions every step
facts.discs: Springy discs lie between the vertebrae

humerus.name: Humerus
humerus.desc: The long bone of the upper arm, from the shoulder joint to the elbow.
humerus.location: The upper arm, between the shoulder blade and the forearm bones

details.type: A long bone.
details.parts: Head, anatomical and surgical necks (the latter a common fracture site), greater and lesser tubercles, shaft and lower end with the trochlea and capitulum. The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle.
details.joints: The shoulder joint with the scapula — the most mobile in the body; the elbow joint with the ulna and radius.
details.muscles: Deltoid, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), brachialis, brachioradialis, forearm flexors and extensors.

facts.funny: Hitting your 'funny bone' means hitting the ulnar nerve at the lower end of this bone
facts.groove: The radial nerve winds around its middle in a spiral groove

ulna.name: Ulna
ulna.desc: The forearm bone on the little-finger side; together with the humerus it forms the elbow joint.
ulna.location: The forearm, on the little-finger side

details.type: A long bone.
details.parts: At the top, the olecranon and coronoid processes with the trochlear notch that grips the humerus; at the bottom, the head and styloid process.
details.joints: The elbow joint and the upper and lower radioulnar joints. It does not join the wrist bones directly — an articular disc lies between them.
details.muscles: Triceps (to the olecranon), brachialis (to the coronoid process), flexor and extensor carpi ulnaris, flexor digitorum profundus.

facts.elbow: Its tip is the point of the elbow you lean on
facts.length: In an adult it is about 25–28 cm long

radius.name: Radius
radius.desc: The forearm bone on the thumb side: when you turn your palm over, it crosses over the ulna.
radius.location: The forearm, on the thumb side

details.type: A long bone.
details.parts: A head with a shallow cup on top, neck, tuberosity (where the biceps attaches), shaft and a broad lower end with the styloid process.
details.joints: The elbow joint, the radioulnar joints (the head spins in the annular ligament as the palm turns) and the wrist joint with the carpal bones.
details.muscles: Biceps, supinator, pronator teres and quadratus, brachioradialis (to the styloid process) and the long muscles of the thumb.

facts.pulse: The pulse at the wrist is felt over the lower end of the radius
facts.fracture: A break at its lower end is one of the most common fractures from falling on a hand

carpals.name: Wrist bones (carpals)
carpals.desc: Eight small bones in two rows between the forearm and the palm that make the wrist flexible.
carpals.location: The wrist, at the base of the hand just below the radius and ulna

details.type: Short spongy bones.
details.parts: Upper row: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform; lower row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate. Together they form a trough — the carpal tunnel.
details.joints: The wrist joint with the radius, the intercarpal joints and the carpometacarpal joints; the saddle joint at the base of the thumb lets it oppose the other fingers.
details.muscles: Tendons of the wrist flexors and extensors (flexor carpi ulnaris attaches to the pisiform) and the short muscles of the thumb and little-finger pads.

facts.scaphoid: The scaphoid breaks most often — in a fall on an outstretched hand
facts.tunnel: The finger flexor tendons and the median nerve run through the carpal tunnel; squeezing them causes carpal tunnel syndrome

metacarpals.name: Palm bones (metacarpals)
metacarpals.desc: Five slender bones of the palm running from the wrist to the fingers.
metacarpals.location: The palm, between the wrist and the fingers; their heads are the knuckles of a fist

details.type: Small long bones.
details.parts: Each has a base (towards the wrist), a shaft and a head (towards the finger); the first metacarpal, of the thumb, is the shortest and thickest.
details.joints: Carpometacarpal joints with the wrist bones and metacarpophalangeal joints with the first phalanges of the fingers.
details.muscles: The interossei (between the metacarpals), the opponens muscles of the thumb and little finger, and the tendons of flexor carpi radialis and the wrist extensors (to their bases).

facts.knuckles: The knuckles of a clenched fist are the heads of the metacarpals
facts.boxer: A break of the neck of the 5th metacarpal is called a “boxer's fracture”

phalanges.name: Finger bones (phalanges)
phalanges.desc: Fourteen small bones of the fingers: three in each finger and two in the thumb.

details.type: Small long bones.
details.parts: Proximal, middle and distal phalanges; the thumb has no middle one. The distal phalanx has a rough tuberosity under the fingertip pad.
details.joints: Metacarpophalangeal joints with the metacarpals and interphalangeal joints — hinge joints, so the fingers only bend and straighten in them.
details.muscles: Tendons of the deep and superficial finger flexors (to the distal and middle phalanges), the finger extensors, the lumbricals and the interossei.

facts.quarter: The two hands hold 54 bones — more than a quarter of all the bones in the body
facts.thumb: The thumb has only two phalanges, yet its saddle joint lets it touch each of the other fingers

pelvis.name: Hip bones
pelvis.desc: Two large bones that form the pelvis together with the sacrum: they carry the weight of the trunk and protect the pelvic organs.
pelvis.location: The bottom of the trunk; the heads of the thigh bones fit into their hip sockets

details.type: Flat bones. In a child each consists of three bones joined by cartilage in the acetabulum; they fuse by the age of 15–17.
details.parts: The ilium (a wing with the iliac crest and anterior superior spine), pubis and ischium (we sit on the ischial tuberosities); between pubis and ischium is the obturator foramen.
details.joints: The sacroiliac joints with the sacrum, the pubic symphysis in front and the hip joints with the femurs.
details.muscles: Gluteal muscles, iliacus, abdominal muscles (to the crest), adductors, hamstrings (to the ischial tuberosity), sartorius and rectus femoris (to the iliac spines).

facts.three: Each hip bone grows together from three: the ilium, the pubis and the ischium
facts.female: A woman's pelvis is wider and shallower, which makes childbirth easier

sacrum.name: Sacrum
sacrum.desc: A triangular bone made of five fused vertebrae that closes the pelvis at the back.
sacrum.location: The bottom of the spine, between the hip bones; the tailbone is below it

details.type: A spongy bone of five fused sacral vertebrae.
details.parts: A base on top with the forward-jutting promontory and an apex below; four pairs of sacral foramina on the front, and inside the sacral canal, a continuation of the vertebral canal.
details.joints: Joints with the 5th lumbar vertebra, the sacroiliac joints with the hip bones and the joint with the coccyx.
details.muscles: Erector spinae, gluteus maximus and piriformis.

facts.fused: Five vertebrae fuse into one bone by the age of 20–25
facts.holes: Nerves to the pelvic organs and legs pass through openings in the sacrum

femur.name: Thigh bone (femur)
femur.desc: The longest and strongest bone in the body: it connects the pelvis to the knee.
femur.location: The thigh; its head fits into the hip joint

details.type: A long bone — the longest in the body.
details.parts: Head, neck (at about 125–130° to the shaft in adults), greater and lesser trochanters, a shaft with the linea aspera at the back and two condyles below.
details.joints: The hip joint with the acetabulum and the knee joint with the tibia and patella.
details.muscles: Gluteal and iliopsoas muscles (to the trochanters), adductors (to the linea aspera), the vasti (from the shaft) and gastrocnemius (from the condyles).

facts.length: It is about a quarter of a person's height
facts.strength: It can bear many times the body's weight
facts.neck: A broken hip, a fracture of its neck, is a common injury in older people

patella.name: Kneecap (patella)
patella.desc: A flat little bone at the front of the knee that shields the joint and helps the quadriceps straighten the leg.
patella.location: The front of the knee — easy to feel under the skin

details.type: A sesamoid bone — the largest in the body: it sits inside the quadriceps tendon.
details.parts: Base (top), apex (bottom), a smooth back joint surface with thick cartilage, and a rough front.
details.joints: The patellofemoral joint with the condyles of the femur — part of the knee joint.
details.muscles: From above, the quadriceps tendon (rectus femoris and the three vasti); from the apex the patellar ligament runs down to the tibia.

facts.lever: Like a pulley, it lengthens the lever of the quadriceps, so straightening the knee is easier
facts.baby: In a newborn the kneecap is cartilage; it turns to bone only at about 3–6 years

tibia.name: Shinbone (tibia)
tibia.desc: The main bone of the lower leg, carrying almost all the body weight from the knee to the foot.
tibia.location: The lower leg, on the big-toe side; its sharp front edge can be felt under the skin

details.type: Long bone — the second longest in the body.
details.parts: Medial and lateral condyles at the top, the tuberosity for the patellar ligament, a triangular shaft with a sharp front edge, and the medial malleolus at the bottom.
details.joints: The knee joint with the femur, the tibiofibular joints with the fibula and the ankle joint with the talus.
details.muscles: Tibialis anterior (on its outer surface), sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus (the pes anserinus), the quadriceps through the patellar ligament, and soleus and tibialis posterior at the back.

facts.shin: Its front edge is hardly covered by muscle, which is why a knock on the shin hurts so much
facts.weight: It takes almost all the load of the lower leg: the fibula carries only about a sixth of the weight

fibula.name: Fibula
fibula.desc: The thin outer bone of the lower leg: it anchors muscles and forms the outer ankle.
fibula.location: The outer side of the lower leg, beside the tibia

details.type: Long bone — slender and carrying little weight.
details.parts: The head at the top, a thin shaft and the lateral malleolus at the bottom; the interosseous membrane joins it to the tibia along its length.
details.joints: The superior tibiofibular joint above and the tibiofibular syndesmosis below; the lateral malleolus is part of the ankle joint.
details.muscles: Fibularis longus and brevis, extensor digitorum longus, soleus and biceps femoris (to the head).

facts.graft: A piece of it can be taken to rebuild bone elsewhere — the leg manages without it
facts.ankle: The outer ankle bump is the lower end of the fibula

foot.name: Bones of the foot
foot.desc: 26 bones of the tarsus, metatarsus and toes that hold the body up on an arch and spring with every step.
foot.location: The foot: 7 tarsal bones, 5 metatarsals and 14 toe bones

details.type: The tarsal bones are short spongy bones; the metatarsals and toe phalanges are small long bones.
details.parts: Tarsus: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms; metatarsus: five metatarsals; the toes have three phalanges each, the big toe two. Together they form the longitudinal and transverse arches.
details.joints: The ankle joint (talus with the tibia and fibula), the subtalar, intertarsal, tarsometatarsal, metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints.
details.muscles: The Achilles tendon of gastrocnemius and soleus (to the calcaneus), tibialis anterior and fibularis longus (to the 1st metatarsal), the toe extensors and flexors and the short muscles of the sole.

facts.arch: The arch of the foot works like a spring: it flattens slightly and recoils with every step
facts.heel: The heel bone is the largest bone of the foot and takes the impact of every step

sternocleidomastoid.name: Sternocleidomastoid
sternocleidomastoid.desc: A neck muscle running from the bump behind the ear to the breastbone and collarbone: it tilts the head and turns it to the side.
sternocleidomastoid.location: The side of the neck; easy to see when you turn your head

details.origin: Two heads — from the manubrium of the sternum and the medial third of the clavicle.
details.insertion: The mastoid process of the temporal bone and the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone.
details.action: One muscle tilts the head towards its shoulder and turns the face to the opposite side; both together flex the neck and raise the sternum during deep breathing.
details.nerve: The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) and branches of the cervical plexus (C2–C3).
details.blood: Branches of the occipital and superior thyroid arteries.

facts.turn: The right muscle turns the head to the left, and the left one to the right
facts.breath: During hard breathing it helps lift the chest

scalenes.name: Scalenes
scalenes.desc: Three muscles on the side of the neck that bend it and lift the first ribs in a deep breath.
scalenes.location: The side of the neck, deeper than the sternocleidomastoid — from the cervical vertebrae to the 1st and 2nd ribs

details.origin: Transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae (C2–C7).
details.insertion: Anterior and middle — the 1st rib; posterior — the 2nd rib.
details.action: Bend the neck to their side, and both sides together flex it forward; with the neck still they raise the 1st and 2nd ribs and help breathing in.
details.nerve: Anterior rami of the cervical spinal nerves (C3–C8).
details.blood: The ascending cervical and inferior thyroid arteries (from the thyrocervical trunk).

facts.gap: The subclavian artery and the brachial plexus pass between the anterior and middle scalenes
facts.breath: When you are out of breath they work as extra muscles of breathing in

sternohyoid.name: Sternohyoid
sternohyoid.desc: A thin strap at the front of the neck that pulls the hyoid bone and larynx down after swallowing.
sternohyoid.location: The front of the neck on either side of the midline — from the breastbone to the hyoid bone

details.origin: The back of the manubrium of the sternum and the sternal end of the clavicle.
details.insertion: The body of the hyoid bone.
details.action: Lowers the hyoid bone, and the larynx with it, after swallowing and in speech; steadies the hyoid when the mouth opens.
details.blood: The superior thyroid artery.

facts.straps: One of the four “strap” muscles of the neck below the hyoid bone
facts.thyroid: It lies right in front of the thyroid gland — surgeons part these muscles to reach it

trapezius.name: Trapezius
trapezius.desc: A large flat muscle of the back and neck: it raises and pulls together the shoulder blades and supports the head.
trapezius.location: The upper back and back of the neck, out to the shoulders

details.origin: The external occipital protuberance, the nuchal ligament and the spinous processes of C7 and all thoracic vertebrae.
details.insertion: The lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula.
details.action: Upper fibres raise the scapula, middle fibres pull it towards the spine, lower fibres lower it; upper and lower fibres together rotate the scapula to lift the arm above shoulder level.
details.nerve: The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) and branches of the cervical plexus (C3–C4).
details.blood: The transverse cervical artery, suprascapular artery and posterior intercostal arteries.

facts.shape: Together the two muscles look like a trapezoid, hence the name
facts.shrug: It is the muscle that lifts your shoulders when you shrug

deltoid.name: Deltoid
deltoid.desc: The muscle that covers the shoulder joint: it lifts the arm out to the side and up.
deltoid.location: The outer side of the shoulder, giving it its rounded shape

details.origin: The lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula — where the trapezius inserts.
details.insertion: The deltoid tuberosity halfway down the outer side of the humerus.
details.action: The middle part raises the arm sideways to shoulder level (supraspinatus starts the movement); the front part flexes and turns the arm inward, the back part extends and turns it outward.
details.nerve: The axillary nerve (C5–C6); it can be injured by a shoulder dislocation or a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus.
details.blood: The posterior circumflex humeral artery and the deltoid branch of the thoracoacromial artery.

facts.delta: It looks like an upside-down Greek letter delta (Δ)

pectoralis.name: Pectoralis major
pectoralis.desc: A fan-shaped chest muscle: it pulls the arm toward the body and turns it inward.
pectoralis.location: The front of the chest, from the breastbone and collarbone to the humerus

details.origin: The clavicular part from the medial half of the clavicle, the sternocostal part from the sternum and cartilages of ribs 1–6, the abdominal part from the rectus sheath.
details.insertion: The crest of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
details.action: Pulls the arm towards the body and turns it inward; the clavicular part raises the arm forward. With the arms braced it helps breathing in.
details.nerve: The lateral and medial pectoral nerves from the brachial plexus (C5–T1).
details.blood: Pectoral branches of the thoracoacromial artery, intercostal arteries and perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery.

facts.pushups: The main muscle in push-ups and the bench press
facts.armpit: Its edge forms the front wall of the armpit

intercostals.name: Intercostal muscles
intercostals.desc: Thin muscles between the ribs that raise and lower them in breathing and close the gaps in the chest wall.
intercostals.location: The spaces between the ribs, in several layers

details.origin: The lower border of the rib above.
details.insertion: The upper border of the rib below (external fibres run down and forward, internal ones down and back).
details.action: The external ones raise the ribs in breathing in, the internal ones lower them in forced breathing out; together they stiffen the chest wall.
details.blood: Intercostal arteries: posterior ones from the aorta, anterior ones from the internal thoracic artery.

facts.layers: Three layers: external, internal and innermost intercostals
facts.groove: The intercostal vessels and nerve run along the lower edge of each rib, sheltered by its groove

biceps.name: Biceps brachii
biceps.desc: The muscle at the front of the upper arm: it bends the elbow and turns the palm up.
biceps.location: The front of the upper arm

details.origin: The long head from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula (its tendon runs through the shoulder joint), the short head from the coracoid process.
details.insertion: The radial tuberosity and, through its aponeurosis, the fascia of the forearm.
details.action: Flexes the elbow, powerfully turns the palm up (supination) and helps raise the arm forward.
details.blood: Muscular branches of the brachial artery.

facts.heads: It starts with two heads, hence the name
facts.partner: Its opponent is the triceps at the back of the arm, which straightens the elbow

brachioradialis.name: Brachioradialis
brachioradialis.desc: A forearm muscle on the thumb side: it bends the elbow, especially with the palm turned sideways.
brachioradialis.location: The outer forearm, from the humerus to the radius

details.origin: The lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.
details.insertion: The base of the styloid process of the radius.
details.action: Flexes the elbow — most strongly with the palm facing sideways — and returns the forearm to this mid position.
details.nerve: The radial nerve (C5–C6), although the other muscles of this nerve are mostly extensors.
details.blood: The radial recurrent artery and branches of the radial artery.

facts.hammer: It works hardest when you hold a hammer or a mug
facts.visible: It shows clearly under the skin when you bend your arm hard

pronator_teres.name: Pronator teres
pronator_teres.desc: A short muscle near the elbow that turns the palm down and helps bend the arm.
pronator_teres.location: The top of the front of the forearm — diagonally from the inner epicondyle of the humerus to the middle of the radius

details.origin: Humeral head — the medial epicondyle of the humerus; ulnar head — the coronoid process of the ulna.
details.insertion: The middle of the outer surface of the radius.
details.action: Turns the forearm palm-down (pronation) and helps bend the elbow.
details.blood: The ulnar and radial arteries and their recurrent branches.

facts.nerve: The median nerve passes between its two heads and can be squeezed there
facts.key: It works when you turn a key in a lock or pour water from a jug

flexor_carpi_radialis.name: Flexor carpi radialis
flexor_carpi_radialis.desc: A muscle on the front of the forearm that bends the hand at the wrist and tilts it towards the thumb.
flexor_carpi_radialis.location: The middle of the front (palm side) of the forearm; its tendon lies at the wrist on the thumb side

details.origin: The medial epicondyle of the humerus (the common flexor tendon).
details.insertion: The bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals.
details.action: Bends the hand at the wrist and tilts it towards the thumb; helps bend the elbow.
details.blood: The radial artery.

facts.pulse: The wrist pulse is felt just outside its tendon, where the radial artery runs
facts.tendon: Its tendon stands out at the wrist when you bend the hand against resistance

flexor_carpi_ulnaris.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
flexor_carpi_ulnaris.desc: A muscle along the inner edge of the forearm that bends the hand at the wrist and tilts it towards the little finger.
flexor_carpi_ulnaris.location: The front of the forearm along the ulna, on the little-finger side

details.origin: The medial epicondyle of the humerus and the back border of the ulna.
details.insertion: The pisiform, the hook of the hamate and the base of the 5th metacarpal.
details.action: Bends the hand at the wrist and tilts it towards the little finger — as when striking with a hammer.
details.blood: The ulnar artery.

facts.nerve: It is the only wrist flexor supplied by the ulnar nerve
facts.pisiform: The pisiform sits inside its tendon, like the kneecap in the quadriceps tendon

rectus_abdominis.name: Rectus abdominis
rectus_abdominis.desc: A long muscle of the front abdominal wall: it bends the trunk forward and tightens the abs.
rectus_abdominis.location: The front of the abdomen from the ribs to the pubic bone, on both sides of the midline

details.origin: The pubic crest and pubic symphysis.
details.insertion: The cartilages of ribs 5–7 and the xiphoid process of the sternum.
details.action: Flexes the trunk, bringing the chest towards the pelvis; raises abdominal pressure when straining, coughing and breathing out forcefully.
details.nerve: The lower intercostal nerves (T7–T11) and the subcostal nerve (T12).
details.blood: The superior epigastric artery (from the internal thoracic) and the inferior epigastric artery (from the external iliac); they join inside the muscle.

facts.cubes: Bands of tendon divide it into the 'six-pack'
facts.cough: It helps with coughing, straining and forceful breathing out

external_oblique.name: External oblique
external_oblique.desc: A broad muscle of the side of the abdomen: it twists and bends the trunk.
external_oblique.location: The sides of the abdomen, running down and forward from the lower ribs

details.origin: The outer surface of the lower eight ribs (5–12), by slips that interlock with those of serratus anterior.
details.insertion: Through a broad aponeurosis to the iliac crest and the linea alba; the thickened lower edge of the aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament.
details.action: One muscle turns the trunk to the opposite side and bends it to its own side; both together flex the trunk and compress the abdomen.
details.nerve: The lower intercostal nerves (T7–T11) and the subcostal nerve (T12).
details.blood: The lower posterior intercostal, subcostal and deep circumflex iliac arteries.

facts.pockets: Its fibers run the same way as your fingers when your hands are in your jacket pockets
facts.layers: Two more muscles lie beneath it: the internal oblique and the transverse abdominis

sartorius.name: Sartorius
sartorius.desc: The longest muscle in the body: a strap that crosses the thigh diagonally and bends the hip and knee.
sartorius.location: The front of the thigh, running diagonally from the pelvis to the inner side of the knee

details.origin: The anterior superior iliac spine.
details.insertion: The medial surface of the upper tibia — as part of the pes anserinus together with gracilis and semitendinosus.
details.action: Flexes, abducts and turns the thigh outward and bends the knee — as in a tailor sitting cross-legged.
details.blood: Muscular branches of the femoral artery.

facts.tailor: It is named after tailors: it helps you sit cross-legged
facts.length: It is about half a meter long

rectus_femoris.name: Rectus femoris
rectus_femoris.desc: One of the four heads of the quadriceps: it straightens the knee and bends the hip.
rectus_femoris.location: The middle of the front of the thigh

details.origin: The anterior inferior iliac spine and the edge of the hip bone above the acetabulum.
details.insertion: Through the common quadriceps tendon to the patella and, via the patellar ligament, to the tibial tuberosity.
details.action: Straightens the knee. The only head of the quadriceps that also crosses the hip, so it flexes the thigh as well.
details.blood: The lateral circumflex femoral artery (a branch of the deep femoral artery).

facts.kick: It works when you kick a ball or climb stairs
facts.quads: The quadriceps is one of the strongest muscles in the body

vastus_lateralis.name: Vastus lateralis
vastus_lateralis.desc: The largest head of the quadriceps: it straightens the knee.
vastus_lateralis.location: The outer side of the thigh

details.origin: The greater trochanter, intertrochanteric line and lateral lip of the linea aspera of the femur.
details.insertion: Via the quadriceps tendon to the patella and the tibial tuberosity.
details.action: Straightens the knee and keeps it locked when standing and walking.
details.blood: The descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery.

facts.injection: Babies get injections and vaccines here
facts.biopsy: It is the usual place to take a small muscle sample for testing

vastus_medialis.name: Vastus medialis
vastus_medialis.desc: The teardrop-shaped muscle above the inner knee that straightens the leg and keeps the kneecap on track.
vastus_medialis.location: The inner side of the thigh above the knee

details.origin: The intertrochanteric line and the medial lip of the linea aspera of the femur.
details.insertion: Through the quadriceps tendon — the patella, and through the patellar ligament — the tibial tuberosity.
details.action: Straightens the knee; its lower oblique fibres pull the kneecap inward and keep it from slipping outward.
details.blood: The femoral and deep femoral arteries.

facts.drop: Its shape above the knee earned it the nickname “teardrop”
facts.rehab: After knee injuries it is one of the first muscles to train — it weakens quickly

adductors.name: Thigh adductors
adductors.desc: A group of muscles on the inner thigh: they bring the legs together.
adductors.location: The inner thigh, from the pubic bone to the femur

details.origin: The pubis and ischium (their rami and the ischial tuberosity).
details.insertion: The whole length of the linea aspera of the femur and the adductor tubercle; gracilis inserts on the tibia.
details.action: Pull the thigh inward and help flex it, while the ischial part of adductor magnus helps extend it; they steady the pelvis when walking.
details.nerve: Mainly the obturator nerve (L2–L4); pectineus is supplied by the femoral nerve and the ischial part of adductor magnus by the sciatic nerve.
details.blood: The deep femoral, obturator and femoral arteries.

facts.riding: They work especially hard in horse riders and footballers
facts.groin: Straining them is a common sports injury of the groin

tibialis_anterior.name: Tibialis anterior
tibialis_anterior.desc: The muscle on the front of the shin that lifts the foot with every step.
tibialis_anterior.location: The front of the lower leg, just outside the sharp edge of the tibia

details.origin: The lateral condyle and upper two thirds of the outer surface of the tibia, and the interosseous membrane.
details.insertion: The medial cuneiform and the base of the 1st metatarsal.
details.action: Lifts the foot (dorsiflexion) and turns the sole inward; in walking it keeps the toes from catching the ground.
details.blood: The anterior tibial artery.

facts.drop: When it is paralysed, the foot slaps and the toes drag — a “foot drop”
facts.shin: Overloading it in running is one cause of shin pain

gastrocnemius.name: Gastrocnemius
gastrocnemius.desc: The powerful calf muscle that lifts the heel and drives the push-off in walking, running and jumping.
gastrocnemius.location: The back of the lower leg — the calf; from the front its inner head shows at the edge of the leg

details.origin: Medial and lateral heads — from the condyles of the femur.
details.insertion: Through the Achilles (calcaneal) tendon — the tuberosity of the heel bone.
details.action: Points the foot — rises onto tiptoe — and helps bend the knee.
details.blood: The sural arteries from the popliteal artery.

facts.achilles: Its Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body
facts.triceps: Together with soleus it forms the triceps surae, the three-headed calf muscle

fibularis_longus.name: Fibularis (peroneus) longus
fibularis_longus.desc: A muscle on the outside of the lower leg that turns the sole outward and supports the arch of the foot.
fibularis_longus.location: The outer side of the lower leg along the fibula; its tendon curves behind the outer ankle

details.origin: The head and upper two thirds of the outer surface of the fibula.
details.insertion: Under the sole — the medial cuneiform and the base of the 1st metatarsal.
details.action: Turns the sole outward (eversion), points the foot and, with tibialis anterior, holds up the transverse arch like a stirrup.
details.blood: The fibular and anterior tibial arteries.

facts.stirrup: It attaches to the same bones as tibialis anterior, only from the other side — together they sling the arch of the foot like a stirrup
facts.sprain: It catches the foot when the ankle rolls; its tendons are often hurt in ankle sprains
